title: C++
tagline: From your first program to expert-level modern C++
description: Thirteen milestones that take you from Hello World to templates, concurrency and performance work. Every lesson has checked practice, and every milestone ends with projects.

milestones.title: First Steps
milestones.blurb: How C++ turns text into a program, your first programs, variables, input and output, functions, multiple files, debugging and compiler settings.

lessons.title: How C++ Works
lessons.summary: You write **text** (source code). A **compiler** translates it into **machine code**. A **linker** joins the pieces into one **program** that your computer runs directly.

lessons.title: Setup and Your First Program
lessons.summary: There is nothing to install. Type the program, press **Run**, read what comes back. Then break it on purpose to see what errors look like.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a Program
lessons.summary: A program is a list of **statements** inside a **function** called `main`. They run from top to bottom. Each statement ends with `;`. Comments are notes for humans.

lessons.title: Variables and Initialization
lessons.summary: A **variable** is a named box in memory that holds one value of one **type**. Always give it a starting value: `int age{ 25 };`

lessons.title: Input and Output
lessons.summary: `std::cout <<` sends values **out** to the screen. `std::cin >>` brings values **in** from the keyboard. The arrows point the way the data moves.

lessons.title: Operators and Expressions Basics
lessons.summary: An **expression** is anything that works out to a value, such as `2 + 3` or `price * count`. **Operators** are the symbols that do the work. One surprise: with whole numbers, `7 / 2` is `3`.

lessons.title: Functions Basics
lessons.summary: A **function** is a named set of instructions you can use again and again. You hand it values (**arguments**), it does its work, and it can hand one value back (the **return value**).

lessons.title: Multiple Files and Headers
lessons.summary: Real programs are split across files. A **header** (`.h`) says **what exists**. A **source file** (`.cpp`) says **how it works**. `#include` the header wherever you need those functions.

lessons.title: Debugging Basics
lessons.summary: A bug is a place where what the program **does** differs from what you **expected**. Debugging is finding that place. Do it with a method: read the message, look at the values, narrow it down.

lessons.title: Compiler Settings, Build Configurations and Undefined Behavior
lessons.summary: Turn compiler **warnings** up and read them. Build in **Debug** while you work and **Release** when you finish. And meet the most important phrase in C++: **undefined behaviour**.

milestones.title: Types and Data
milestones.blurb: What data really is in memory: integers, floating point, bool, char, conversions, const and constexpr, strings and bit manipulation.

lessons.title: Memory, Bits and Fundamental Types
lessons.summary: Memory is a long row of numbered **bytes**. A byte is 8 **bits**. A variable's **type** decides how many bytes it gets and what the bits in them mean.

lessons.title: Integers
lessons.summary: Integers hold whole numbers. **Signed** ones can be negative; **unsigned** ones cannot. Going past the limit is **overflow**: unsigned wraps round to the other end, and signed is undefined behaviour.

lessons.title: Floating Point Numbers
lessons.summary: `float` and `double` store decimals **approximately**. `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. Use `double` by default, never compare with `==`, and never use them where every cent must be exact.

lessons.title: bool and char
lessons.summary: `bool` holds `true` or `false`, stored as 1 or 0. `char` holds one character, stored as a small number: `'A'` is 65.

lessons.title: Type Conversion and static_cast
lessons.summary: C++ converts between types automatically when it has to. Some conversions **lose information**. When you want a conversion, say so with `static_cast<Type>(value)`.

lessons.title: const and constexpr
lessons.summary: `const` means "this value never changes after it is set". `constexpr` means "this value is known **while compiling**". Use them wherever you can: they prevent mistakes and cost nothing.

lessons.title: Strings — std::string and std::string_view
lessons.summary: `std::string` **owns** its text and can change it. `std::string_view` is a cheap, read-only **window** onto text that lives somewhere else. Functions that only read text should take a `std::string_view`.

lessons.title: Operators Deep Dive
lessons.summary: Comparisons (`==`, `<` ...) produce a `bool`. Logical operators (`&&`, `||`, `!`) combine bools and stop early when the answer is settled. `++x` and `x++` differ in the value they give back. `?:` chooses between two values.

lessons.title: Bit Manipulation
lessons.summary: Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of a number: `&` AND, `|` OR, `^` XOR, `~` NOT, `<<` and `>>` shift. They let you pack many on/off settings into one number and pull packed values apart.

milestones.title: Control Flow and Scope
milestones.blurb: Making decisions and repeating work: if, switch, loops, random numbers, scope, namespaces, linkage, input validation and testing.

lessons.title: if and else
lessons.summary: `if (condition) { ... }` runs a block only when the condition is true. `else if` adds further choices and `else` catches everything left. Only the first branch that matches runs.

lessons.title: switch
lessons.summary: `switch` compares **one** value against a list of fixed options and jumps to the matching `case`. End each case with `break`, or execution carries on into the next one.

lessons.title: Loops — while, do-while, for
lessons.summary: Loops repeat code. `while` repeats as long as a condition holds. `do-while` runs the body at least once. `for` is built for counting. `break` leaves a loop and `continue` skips to the next round.

lessons.title: Random Numbers
lessons.summary: Create **one** random engine, **seed** it once, and use a **distribution** to turn its output into numbers in the range you want. Never create a new engine each time you need a number.

lessons.title: Scope, Lifetime and Namespaces
lessons.summary: **Scope** is *where in the code* a name can be used. **Lifetime** is *when during the run* the variable exists. **Namespaces** group names so that two things called the same do not clash.

lessons.title: Global Variables, static and Linkage
lessons.summary: Globals exist for the whole run of the program. **Linkage** decides whether other `.cpp` files can see a name. A `static` local keeps its value between calls. Avoid globals that can change.

lessons.title: Input Validation and assert
lessons.summary: People type things you did not expect. When `std::cin >> number` receives letters it enters a **fail state**: you must `clear()` it and discard the bad input. Use `assert` to catch mistakes in *your own* code while developing.

tasks.title: Ask until it is a number

lessons.title: Halts, goto, and Testing Your Code
lessons.summary: `std::exit` ends the program from anywhere; `std::abort` ends it at once with no clean-up. `goto` exists and you almost never want it. **Testing** each function with known inputs as you write it is the cheapest way to catch bugs.

milestones.title: Functions and Compound Types
milestones.blurb: Overloading, function templates, references, pointers, enums, structs and type deduction.

lessons.title: Function Overloading and Default Arguments
lessons.summary: **Overloading** gives several functions the same name with different parameters, and the compiler picks the best match for each call. **Default arguments** supply a value when the caller leaves a parameter out.

lessons.title: Function Templates
lessons.summary: A **template** is a pattern for a function with a placeholder type `T`. The compiler generates a real function for each type you use it with. Write it once and it works for `int`, `double`, `std::string` and more.

lessons.title: References
lessons.summary: A **reference** is a second name for an existing variable. Pass by reference to let a function change the caller's variable. Pass by **const reference** to avoid copying something large.

lessons.title: Pointers
lessons.summary: A **pointer** is a variable that stores a **memory address**. `&x` gives the address of `x`. `*ptr` follows the address to the value. Unlike a reference, a pointer can be `nullptr` and can be aimed at something else.

lessons.title: Enums
lessons.summary: An **enum** is a type with a fixed list of named values, such as `enum class Color { red, green, blue };`. Use **`enum class`**: its names stay inside the enum and it does not silently turn into a number.

lessons.title: Structs
lessons.summary: A **struct** bundles related variables into one new type, such as `struct Player { std::string name; int hp; };`. Reach the members with `.`, or `->` through a pointer. Pass structs by `const&`.

lessons.title: auto, Type Deduction and Type Aliases
lessons.summary: `auto` asks the compiler to work out a variable's type from its initializer. `using Name = Type;` gives a type a second name. Both shorten code; use them where the type is obvious or noisy.

milestones.title: Containers and Algorithms
milestones.blurb: vector, array, C-style arrays, iterators, standard algorithms, lambdas, grids, recursion, function pointers, sorting and Big-O.

lessons.title: std::vector Basics
lessons.summary: `std::vector<T>` is a **resizable list** of elements stored side by side in memory. Reach elements with `v[i]` (fast, unchecked) or `v.at(i)` (checked). It is the container to reach for first.

lessons.title: Looping Over Containers
lessons.summary: Use the **range-based for loop**, `for (const auto& x : v)`, whenever you need each element. Use an index loop when you need the position too. Remember that `v.size()` is **unsigned**.

lessons.title: Vector as a Stack, and Capacity
lessons.summary: A vector has a **size** (elements in use) and a **capacity** (room reserved). When it runs out of room it reallocates. `push_back`, `pop_back` and `back` make it a natural **stack**: last in, first out.

lessons.title: Fixed-Size Arrays — std::array
lessons.summary: `std::array<T, N>` is an array whose length `N` is fixed at **compile time**. It cannot grow, needs no separate memory block, and can be `constexpr`. Use it when the count never changes.

lessons.title: C-Style Arrays and C-Strings
lessons.summary: `int arr[5]{};` is the raw array inherited from C. Passed to a function it **decays** to a pointer and loses its length. A C-string is a `char` array ending in `'\0'`. Learn them to read existing code; write `std::array`, `std::vector` and `std::string`.

lessons.title: Iterators and STL Algorithms
lessons.summary: An **iterator** marks a position in a container. `begin()` is the first element and `end()` is **one past the last**. The `<algorithm>` library supplies tested functions (`sort`, `find`, `count` and many more) that work on any such range.

lessons.title: Lambdas
lessons.summary: A **lambda** is a function written inline, right where it is needed, such as `[](int x) { return x * 2; }`. Its **capture list** `[ ]` lets it use variables from the surrounding code. Lambdas are how you customise algorithms.

lessons.title: 2D Arrays and Grids
lessons.summary: A grid is an array **of arrays**, indexed `grid[row][col]`. Use nested `std::array` for fixed sizes, a vector of vectors for sizes decided while running, or one flat vector indexed by `row * width + col`.

tasks.title: One step of the Game of Life

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.summary: A **recursive** function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. It needs a **base case** that stops, and a **recursive case** that moves towards it. Every call gets its own set of local variables.

lessons.title: Function Pointers, Callbacks and Command-Line Arguments
lessons.summary: Functions live in memory too, so a pointer can refer to one. A **function pointer** lets you pass "which function to call" as an argument: a **callback**. Modern C++ mostly uses lambdas, but C interfaces use function pointers. Also here: reading a program's command-line arguments.

tasks.title: Sort with a rule passed in

lessons.title: Sorting, Searching, Big-O and Timing Your Code
lessons.summary: See how sorting and searching actually work, describe their speed with **Big-O** notation, and measure real time with `<chrono>`. Then use `std::sort` in real code.

milestones.title: Classes and Objects
milestones.blurb: Object-oriented programming: classes, constructors, destructors, const members, statics, friends and operator overloading.

lessons.title: Classes and Objects
lessons.summary: A **class** combines **data** (member variables) with the **functions** that work on it (member functions). The data is usually `private`, and the public functions are the only way in. That protection is called **encapsulation**.

lessons.title: Constructors
lessons.summary: A **constructor** is a special member function that runs when an object is created and puts it in a valid state. Initialize members in a **member initializer list**. Know the default, delegating, converting (`explicit`) and copy constructors.

tasks.title: A date that is always valid

lessons.title: Destructors and Object Lifetime
lessons.summary: A **destructor**, `~ClassName()`, runs automatically when an object's life ends. Use it to release what the object holds: files, memory, locks. Objects are destroyed in the **reverse** order of their creation.

lessons.title: this, const Member Functions and Chaining
lessons.summary: Inside a member function, `this` points at the object the function was called on. Mark every function that does not modify the object `const`: only those can be called on `const` objects. Return `*this` by reference to allow **chaining**.

lessons.title: Static Members and Friends
lessons.summary: A **static member** belongs to the **class itself** and is shared by all its objects. A **friend** is a function or class that has been granted access to another class's private members.

lessons.title: Classes in Header Files and Nested Types
lessons.summary: Put the **class definition** in `Name.h` and the **member function bodies** in `Name.cpp`, written as `ClassName::function`. Small functions can stay in the header. Types can be nested inside a class, as in `Player::State`.

tasks.title: A stack class in two files

lessons.title: Operator Overloading Basics
lessons.summary: Operators can be taught to work with your own types, so that `a + b`, `a == b` and `std::cout << a` all make sense. An operator is simply a function named `operator+`. Use non-member functions for symmetric operators, and `= default` for comparisons.

lessons.title: Operator Overloading — Advanced
lessons.summary: The remaining operators: unary (`-x`, `!x`), increment and decrement in prefix and postfix form, subscript `[]`, the function-call operator `()`, conversions such as `explicit operator bool`, and assignment `=`.

lessons.title: Designing Good Classes
lessons.summary: A good class has **one clear job**, a **small public interface that is hard to misuse**, **protects its invariants** and is **const-correct**. Design it from the point of view of the code that will use it.

milestones.title: Memory Management
milestones.blurb: Stack and heap, new and delete, deep copies, RAII, move semantics, smart pointers, object relationships and container classes.

lessons.title: Stack vs Heap
lessons.summary: A program's memory has regions. The **stack** holds local variables: very fast and automatic, but small and tied to scope. The **heap** holds memory requested while running: large and flexible, but something has to manage it.

tasks.title: Do not return a local by reference
Recursion that runs out of stack

lessons.title: new and delete — Dynamic Memory
lessons.summary: `new` allocates on the heap and returns a pointer; `delete` releases it. Arrays use `new[]` and `delete[]`. Each `new` needs exactly **one** matching `delete`. Forget it and you **leak**. Do it twice and you corrupt the heap. Use the memory afterwards and the pointer **dangles**.

tasks.title: A box that cleans up after itself

lessons.title: Copy Semantics — Shallow vs Deep
lessons.summary: The default copy copies each member, and for a pointer that means the **address**, not the data. Two objects then own one block of memory and both delete it. A class that owns a resource needs a **copy constructor** and a **copy assignment operator** that make a **deep copy**.

lessons.title: RAII and the Rule of Three
lessons.summary: **RAII**: tie every resource to an object's lifetime. Acquire it in the constructor and release it in the destructor, and clean-up becomes automatic on every path. **Rule of Three**: a class that needs a destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment operator almost certainly needs all three.

tasks.title: Run this when the scope ends

lessons.title: Move Semantics
lessons.summary: Copying a large object duplicates its data. **Moving** transfers the data out of an object that is about to disappear, by handing over a few pointers. **Rvalue references**, written `T&&`, bind to such objects, and `std::move` lets you mark one as movable.

lessons.title: Smart Pointers
lessons.summary: Smart pointers are RAII wrappers that delete a heap object automatically. `std::unique_ptr` has **one owner** and is the default. `std::shared_ptr` shares ownership by counting references. `std::weak_ptr` observes without owning. Create them with `std::make_unique` and `std::make_shared`.

tasks.title: A tree that does not leak

lessons.title: Object Relationships
lessons.summary: Objects relate in a few standard ways. **Composition**: a part that is owned and dies with the whole. **Aggregation**: has it, but does not own it. **Association**: knows about it. **Dependency**: uses it briefly. Which one applies decides how you store the member.

lessons.title: Container Classes and std::initializer_list
lessons.summary: A **container class** holds and manages a collection, like a small `std::vector` of your own. Building one brings together the whole milestone: heap memory, RAII, the Rule of Five and operators. `std::initializer_list` lets it accept `{ 1, 2, 3 }`.

tasks.title: Braces and range-for for your own class

milestones.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
milestones.blurb: Inheritance, virtual functions, vtables, abstract classes, interfaces, slicing, casting and multiple inheritance.

lessons.title: Inheritance Basics
lessons.summary: **Inheritance** defines a new class (the derived class) from an existing one (the base class), reusing its members and adding more. It models **is-a**: a `Dog` *is an* `Animal`. The base part is constructed first and destroyed last.

lessons.title: Inheritance and Access
lessons.summary: `protected` members are visible to derived classes but not to outside code. The kind of inheritance (`public`, `protected`, `private`) caps how inherited members appear. A derived class can **add** functions, **hide** base ones, **extend** them by calling the base version, or **change their access**.

lessons.title: Virtual Functions and Polymorphism
lessons.summary: A `virtual` function called through a **base pointer or reference** runs the version belonging to the object's actual class. That is **polymorphism**: one interface, many behaviours. Mark overrides with `override`, and give polymorphic base classes a `virtual` destructor.

tasks.title: The destructor must be virtual too

lessons.title: How Virtual Works — vtables
lessons.summary: Ordinary calls are resolved at **compile time** (early binding). Virtual calls are resolved at **run time** (late binding) through a hidden pointer in each object, the `vptr`, to a per-class table of function addresses, the `vtable`. The cost is one pointer per object and one indirection per call.

lessons.title: Abstract Classes and Interfaces
lessons.summary: A **pure virtual** function, declared `= 0`, has no implementation in the base: derived classes **must** supply one. A class with any pure virtual function is **abstract** and cannot be instantiated. A class made only of pure virtual functions is an **interface**: a contract.

tasks.title: Fill in the blanks of an algorithm

lessons.title: Object Slicing, Casting and Composition
lessons.summary: Copying a derived object into a base **value** discards the derived part: that is **slicing**. `dynamic_cast` converts down a hierarchy safely, but needing it often points to a design problem. And the standing advice: **favour composition over inheritance**.

lessons.title: Multiple Inheritance and Virtual Base Classes
lessons.summary: A class may inherit from several bases. That works well for combining **interfaces**. When two bases share a common base, the result is the **diamond problem**, which `virtual` inheritance solves. Use it sparingly.

milestones.title: Templates and Exceptions
milestones.blurb: Class templates, specialisation, variadic templates, concepts, exceptions and exception safety.

lessons.title: Class Templates
lessons.summary: A **class template** is a pattern for classes, parameterized by type: `Box<int>`, `Box<std::string>`. It is how `std::vector<T>` works. The compiler can often deduce the arguments (**CTAD**), and **alias templates** give long instantiations short names.

lessons.title: Non-Type Parameters and Template Specialization
lessons.summary: Templates can take **values** as well as types, as in `template <int N>`: that is how `std::array<T, N>` knows its size. **Specialization** supplies a custom version for particular arguments: **full** (`Box<bool>`) or **partial** (`Box<T*>`).

tasks.title: A size baked into the type

lessons.title: Variadic Templates and Fold Expressions
lessons.summary: A **variadic template** accepts any number of arguments of any types, written `template <typename... Args>`. The arguments form a **parameter pack**, which you expand with `args...`. **Fold expressions** apply an operator across a whole pack in one expression.

tasks.title: Print anything, any number of things

lessons.title: Concepts (C++20)
lessons.summary: A **concept** is a named compile-time requirement on template arguments, such as "T must be a number" or "T must be printable". Constrained templates give **clear error messages** and let you overload on what a type *can do*. They live in `<concepts>`.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.summary: When a function cannot do its job, it **throws** an exception. Control leaves the function and travels up the call stack, running destructors on the way (**stack unwinding**), to the nearest matching **catch**. Throw by value, catch by `const&`, and derive your exception types from `std::exception`.

lessons.title: Exception Safety, noexcept and std::expected
lessons.summary: Code must leave objects in a sensible state when an exception passes through it. Know the **three guarantees**: basic, strong and nothrow. Mark functions that cannot throw `noexcept`. Destructors must not throw. For failures that are a normal outcome, consider `std::optional` or `std::expected`.

tasks.title: A value or the reason why not

milestones.title: Modern C++ and the STL
milestones.blurb: Choosing containers, maps and sets, ranges, optional, variant and tuple, streams, files, std::format, chrono and CMake.

lessons.title: Choosing STL Containers
lessons.summary: The standard library offers **sequence** containers (ordered by position), **associative** containers (sorted by key), **unordered** containers (hash tables) and **adaptors** (stack, queue, priority queue). Default to `std::vector`, and switch only when a specific operation needs to be faster.

tasks.title: First in, first out; biggest first

lessons.title: Maps and Sets
lessons.summary: A **map** stores **key to value** pairs, like a dictionary. A **set** stores unique values. `std::map` and `std::set` keep their keys **sorted**, in a tree with O(log n) operations. `std::unordered_map` and `std::unordered_set` **hash** their keys: O(1) on average, with no order.

lessons.title: Ranges and Views (C++20/23)
lessons.summary: **Ranges** let you pass a whole container to an algorithm, as in `std::ranges::sort(v)`. **Views** are lazy, cheap pipelines such as `v | filter(...) | transform(...) | take(5)`: nothing is computed until you iterate. They live in `<ranges>`.

lessons.title: std::optional, std::variant, std::any and std::tuple
lessons.summary: **Vocabulary types** that say what you mean. `optional<T>` is maybe a T. `variant<A, B, C>` is exactly one of A, B or C. `any` is anything at all. `tuple<A, B, C>` is an A *and* a B *and* a C, without names. `pair` is a tuple of two.

lessons.title: Streams In Depth — istream, ostream, stringstream
lessons.summary: A **stream** is a sequence of characters flowing in or out. The console, files and strings share one interface, so the same `<<` and `>>` code works for all of them. This lesson covers formatting **manipulators**, **stream states** and **string streams** for parsing.

lessons.title: Files and std::filesystem
lessons.summary: `std::ofstream` writes files, `std::ifstream` reads them and `std::fstream` does both. They are RAII types, closed automatically. Text and binary modes differ. `seekg` and `seekp` move around a file. `std::filesystem` handles paths, directories and file information.

lessons.title: Formatting with std::format and std::print
lessons.summary: `std::format("Hello, {}!", name)` builds a string from `{}` placeholders: type-safe, fast and readable. `std::print` and `std::println` (C++23) write directly. Format specifications such as `{:>8.2f}` control width, alignment and precision.

lessons.title: Time and std::chrono
lessons.summary: `<chrono>` models time with three ideas: **durations** (how long), **clocks** (where time comes from) and **time points** (a moment on a clock). The types make unit mistakes impossible. C++20 adds **calendar dates**, **time zones** and formatting.

lessons.title: CMake, Libraries and Package Managers
lessons.summary: Real projects have many files and use third-party libraries. **CMake** describes *what* to build portably and generates the build files for your tools. Libraries are **static** (copied into your executable) or **dynamic** (loaded while running). **vcpkg** and **Conan** download libraries for you.

milestones.title: Advanced Templates and Metaprogramming
milestones.blurb: Perfect forwarding, type traits, SFINAE, compile-time programming, CRTP, type erasure and template metaprogramming.

lessons.title: Value Categories and Perfect Forwarding
lessons.summary: Every expression has a **type** and a **value category**: lvalue, xvalue or prvalue. In a template, `T&&` is a **forwarding reference**: it binds to anything and records whether the argument was an lvalue or an rvalue. `std::forward<T>(x)` passes it on with that category intact, which is **perfect forwarding**.

lessons.title: Type Traits
lessons.summary: **Type traits**, in `<type_traits>`, are compile-time questions about types and transformations of them: "is T an integer?", "T without its const". Each is a template yielding a `value` or a `type`. With `if constexpr` and `static_assert`, they let code adapt to the types it is given.

tasks.title: One function, many kinds of type

lessons.title: SFINAE, enable_if and Tag Dispatch
lessons.summary: **SFINAE**, "Substitution Failure Is Not An Error": if substituting a type into a template's *declaration* produces invalid code, that overload is silently removed instead of causing an error. Code before C++20 used it, through `std::enable_if`, `void_t` and tag dispatch, to constrain templates. **Concepts** do the job better now, but you must be able to read it.

lessons.title: Compile-Time Programming — constexpr, consteval, constinit
lessons.summary: Modern C++ can run real code **inside the compiler**: loops, `std::vector`, `std::string`, even `new` and `delete`, provided nothing allocated escapes to run time. `constexpr` *may* run at compile time, `consteval` *must*, and `constinit` guarantees a static variable is initialized at compile time while leaving it mutable.

lessons.title: CRTP, Mixins and Static Polymorphism
lessons.summary: The **Curiously Recurring Template Pattern**: `class Derived : public Base<Derived>`. The base knows the derived type at compile time, so it can call derived functions **without `virtual`**. That is static polymorphism. It suits mixins and interfaces with no run-time overhead. C++23's **deducing `this`** simplifies it.

tasks.title: A mixin that writes operators for you

lessons.title: Type Erasure
lessons.summary: **Type erasure** hides many unrelated concrete types behind one non-template interface, without requiring them to share a base class. `std::function`, `std::any` and the deleter of `std::shared_ptr` all use it. The recipe: an internal abstract **Concept**, a templated **Model** that wraps any type, and an outer wrapper with value semantics.

lessons.title: Template Metaprogramming Techniques
lessons.summary: **Template metaprogramming** treats types as data and templates as functions that run in the compiler. The core tools are type lists, `std::index_sequence`, recursive instantiation, fold expressions and `if constexpr`. They are what `std::tuple`, `std::variant`, serialization libraries and expression templates are built from.

milestones.title: Concurrency and Coroutines
milestones.blurb: Threads, mutexes, condition variables, futures, atomics and the memory model, parallel algorithms and coroutines.

lessons.title: Threads and std::jthread
lessons.summary: A **thread** is an independent path of execution; several can run at the same time on different processor cores. `std::thread` starts one and must be joined. `std::jthread` (C++20) joins automatically and supports **cooperative cancellation** through `std::stop_token`. Both are in `<thread>`.

lessons.title: Data Races, Mutexes and Locks
lessons.summary: When two threads access the same data, at least one writes, and nothing synchronizes them, you have a **data race**: undefined behaviour. A **mutex** admits one thread at a time to a **critical section**. Lock it with RAII: `std::lock_guard`, `std::scoped_lock`, `std::unique_lock`. Beware **deadlock**.

lessons.title: Condition Variables, Semaphores, Latches and Barriers
lessons.summary: Mutexes protect data. These tools let threads **wait for each other**. A `std::condition_variable` sleeps until told that something changed. C++20 adds `std::counting_semaphore` (limit concurrent access), `std::latch` (a one-shot countdown) and `std::barrier` (a reusable meeting point).

lessons.title: Futures, Promises, std::async and Thread Pools
lessons.summary: A **future** is a handle to a result that will be available later. `std::async(f)` runs `f`, possibly on another thread, and returns a future; `get()` waits for the value, or rethrows the exception. A **promise** is the writing end of the same channel. `std::packaged_task` wraps a callable for use in thread pools.

tasks.title: Results and failures through a future

lessons.title: Atomics and the Memory Model
lessons.summary: `std::atomic<T>` makes individual operations on a variable indivisible, so counters and flags need no mutex. The **memory model** defines what other threads are guaranteed to *observe*: compilers and processors reorder work, and **memory orders** constrain that. The default, `seq_cst`, is the safest; weaken it only with proof.

lessons.title: Parallel Algorithms and SIMD
lessons.summary: Most standard algorithms accept an **execution policy** as their first argument, as in `std::sort(std::execution::par, v.begin(), v.end())`. The library then divides the work across cores, and SIMD lanes, for you. The functions you pass must be safe to run concurrently. The policies are in `<execution>`.

lessons.title: Coroutines (C++20) and std::generator (C++23)
lessons.summary: A **coroutine** is a function that can **suspend** and later **resume**, keeping its local variables in between. Any function containing `co_yield`, `co_await` or `co_return` is one. They serve **generators** (lazy sequences) and **asynchronous code** that reads from top to bottom. `std::generator` makes generators easy; asynchronous types come from a library.

milestones.title: Expert C++
milestones.blurb: Undefined behaviour, memory layout, allocators, performance, modules, the preprocessor, name lookup, idioms, tooling and what comes next.

lessons.title: Undefined Behavior and Object Lifetime
lessons.summary: The compiler optimizes on the assumption that your program has **no undefined behaviour**. Break that assumption and it may delete checks, reorder code, or mis-compile something far from the fault. This lesson is the full catalogue, the rules of object lifetime, and the tools that keep you inside the lines.

tasks.title: Three ways to step off the edge

lessons.title: Memory Layout, Alignment, Unions and Bit Fields
lessons.summary: Every type has a **size** and an **alignment**: its address must be a multiple of the alignment. The compiler inserts **padding** to arrange that. **Unions** overlay members in the same memory. **Bit fields** pack members into bits. **Endianness** fixes the byte order. All of it matters for performance, file formats, networking and hardware.

lessons.title: Custom Memory: Placement new, Allocators and PMR
lessons.summary: `new` does two things: it obtains raw memory **and** constructs an object in it. The two can be separated. **Placement new**, or `std::construct_at`, constructs in memory you already have. Custom **allocators** and **PMR** (polymorphic memory resources) let containers draw their memory from arenas, pools or the stack.

tasks.title: Construct in memory you already have

lessons.title: Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design
lessons.summary: Modern processors are fast and **memory is slow**. Performance comes from keeping data in the **cache**: contiguous arrays, predictable access, small hot data. **Measure first**, optimize the hot spot, and measure again. Data-oriented design arranges data around how it is processed.

lessons.title: Modules (C++20) and import std (C++23)
lessons.summary: **Modules** replace header files: you `export` what is public and `import` it elsewhere. A module is compiled **once**, leaks no macros and has no include-order problems. C++23's `import std;` brings in the whole standard library in one line.

lessons.title: Preprocessor Deep Dive, Attributes and User-Defined Literals
lessons.summary: The preprocessor is a text-substitution engine that runs before compilation: powerful, and blind to types and scope. Know macros, conditional compilation, `#` and `##`, and X-macros, and when *not* to use them. **Attributes** give the compiler extra information. **User-defined literals** let you write `5_km`.

tasks.title: Tell the compiler what you meant

lessons.title: Name Lookup, ADL, Inline Namespaces and the ODR
lessons.summary: How does the compiler decide what a name refers to? **Unqualified lookup** searches outwards through scopes. **ADL** also searches the namespaces of the arguments' types, which is why `std::cout << x` finds `std::operator<<`. **Inline namespaces** version an interface. The **One Definition Rule** keeps definitions consistent across the program.

lessons.title: C++ Idioms and Design Patterns
lessons.summary: **Idioms** are solutions specific to C++: RAII, pImpl, copy and swap, the Rule of Zero, CRTP, type erasure. **Design patterns** are recipes that apply in any language: Strategy, Observer, Factory, Visitor. Knowing their names lets you design faster and talk to other programmers.

lessons.title: Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling
lessons.summary: Professional C++ is supported by tools. **Unit tests** check behaviour. **Sanitizers** catch undefined behaviour as the program runs. **Static analysis** finds defects without running it. **Formatters**, **fuzzers** and **continuous integration** apply all of it to every change.

lessons.title: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next
lessons.summary: C++ gets a new standard every three years. Knowing what arrived when helps you read older code, choose compiler settings and know what you can rely on. After that: pick a field and go deep.
